extracted.intended_audience: geometers, editors/translators of Euclid, and students learning Euclidean geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical notes for editing, translating, and teaching Euclid's Elements: identifying spurious insertions, restoring correct definitions/enunciations, and choosing demonstrations appropriate for learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not place proved propositions among definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions must not state as self-evident what is in fact a theorem (e.g., the 10th definition of Book XI was actually a theorem and ought to be demonstrated, not defined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a statement's truth or falsehood requires demonstration, it should be treated as a proposition to be proved (see discussion of DEF. X, B. XI). Editors who turn theorems into definitions are to be criticised and corrected; equality of figures should be demonstrated from axioms or prior propositions rather than defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplicate statements across books (cancel redundant items)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition demonstrated in one place should not be reintroduced as a definition or repeated as a demonstrated fact elsewhere (e.g., the 5th definition of Book VI repeats Proposition 5 of Book VIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the same proposition appears both as a definition and is demonstrated elsewhere, one occurrence should be cancelled to avoid absurd repetition; determine which placement is original/appropriate and remove the spurious one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original philological nuance in translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain words whose change alters meaning (e.g., Euclid's use of the phrase 'is said to have' was translated wrongly by some as 'has').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep 'is said to have' where the original uses it, rather than translating to 'has'; note and correct mistranslations that change logical force of definitions or demonstrations (examples: Commandine's translation errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions must be precise and not assume what must be proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (e.g., of similar solid figures, equal figures) should state meanings only; they must not incorporate propositions whose truth needs proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend definitions that covertly assert propositions (such as equality results) and instead provide proofs from axioms or earlier propositions (see DEF. IX–X and the discussion on equality of figures).

rubrics_metrics.name: State similitude conditions correctly (angles + proportional sides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similitude of plane figures should be defined from equality of angles and proportionality of the sides about those angles; either condition alone does not suffice except for triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly require both angle equality and the proportionality of corresponding sides for plane figures (note the special case where triangles require only one of the conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark non-original additions and spurious insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and note parts of the text that are later additions (e.g., Theon's additions, 'because they are at the centre' left in by an unskilful hand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a passage is demonstrably an editor's addition, indicate this in notes and consider removing or flagging it; similarly omit illative particles or inserted words that do not belong in the authentic demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration of omitted necessary words
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Greek or Latin manuscripts omit words that are necessary to the sense (e.g., the words 'any whatever' omitted in demonstrations), restore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare textual witnesses and add back words that are required for generality or correctness of enunciation/demonstration; conversely, remove words that appear to be later interpolations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure enunciations are general enough to cover all cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Enunciations must be stated in sufficiently general form to include all relevant configurations (e.g., the 26th proposition's preceding enunciation was not general enough to include vertically opposite angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proposition applies to multiple geometric configurations, phrase the enunciation to encompass them (add cases like vertically opposite angles or similarly placed parallelograms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer demonstrations appropriate for beginners (balance brevity and pedagogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: While shorter demonstrations (e.g., Candalla's) may be elegant, retain or supply longer demonstrations that show constructive methods useful to learners (for instance, how to find a ratio compounded of given ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing between a short proof that omits constructive detail and a longer one that teaches methods, include the longer for pedagogical benefit or retain both with commentary explaining the shorter proof's omitted steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the purpose and proper use of compound ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound ratio is chiefly a notational/name device to avoid circumlocution; it expresses the ratio of the first to the last and simultaneously indicates the intermediate ratios (which need not be equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify that compound ratio is optional shorthand — propositions can be enunciated and proved without it — but when used, also demonstrate how to find the compounded ratio so beginners learn the procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish compound, duplicate, and triplicate ratios precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate/triplicate ratios are names indicating that intermediate ratios are equal, whereas compound ratio does not require intervening ratios to be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve Euclid's original distinctions and wording; explain that 'duplicate' means two equal intermediate ratios, 'triplicate' three, whereas 'compounded' simply denotes the ratio of first to last and the intermediate chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid composing demonstrations out of mismatched sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not patch together two separate demonstrations into one in a way that introduces superfluous or irrelevant steps (several propositions' demonstrations show signs of being made up from two others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a proof appears to be an amalgam, reconstruct a coherent, minimal demonstration (and note where composition occurred); prefer simpler direct proofs and remove needless detours that obscure the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not omit frequently used problems or propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems/propositions that are widely used by geometers (e.g., Props. XXVIII and XXIX, used in many solutions) should not be omitted from editions on the pretext of being 'scarce of use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain such general and useful problems for the benefit of practitioners and learners; annotate their frequent applications to justify inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent lettering/labeling across multiple cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting multiple cases of a problem, use the same letters for corresponding points/lines (the second case had different letters and should be marked with the same ones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent labels reduce confusion; if earlier editors changed letters, correct them so that cases align and readers can follow correspondences between diagrams and text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include necessary intermediate steps (e.g., inversion of proportionals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not omit crucial logical moves required to reach a conclusion legitimately (the inversion of proportionals was twice neglected and must be added to make use of a referenced proposition valid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referencing another proposition to conclude a result, ensure all requisite intermediate transformations are present; add missing inversions/compositions and note such corrections in the commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer demonstrations that show how to compute geometric quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a short proof omits the method to compute or find an object (e.g., Candalla's proof does not show how to find the ratio compounded of two given ratios), include demonstrations that explicitly show constructive methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the didactic edition, retain or add steps that teach the technique (so beginners learn how to 'find the ratio which is compounded of two or more given ratios').

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag and correct erroneous generalizations about solids
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assert universal propositions about solids (e.g., that solids contained by the same number of similar plane faces are equal) without proof — counterexamples show this is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide counterexamples and corollaries to demonstrate false generalizations (as done with the two unequal solids composed around different vertices), and amend definitions/theorems accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain useful supplementary propositions that editors added later
rubrics_metrics.description: Some added propositions (three appended propositions in Book VI) are frequently used by geometers and should be kept rather than summarily removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When later additions are demonstrably useful, include them with annotations identifying their later origin and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with permutation in proportion arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Permutation is sometimes used incorrectly (moderns frequently commit this mistake); remove unjustified permutations and rely on established results when concluding equalities among proportionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using permutation to conclude equality of non-adjacent terms unless a demonstrated proposition justifies it; point out repeated occurrences of the same blunder in the text and correct them.
